prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat as simple otitis media relapse or attribute the syndrome solely to the prior ear infection without confirming or excluding meningitis by CSF analysis.
Do not delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting LP or imaging when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not discontinue dexamethasone because the ear infection was treated previously; the 4-day course targets current meningeal inflammation.

Do not rely on a negative or mild ear examination to exclude bacterial meningitis; the otic focus may be clinically subtle once the acute ear infection resolves but the intracranial seeding has occurred.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Perform lumbar puncture and send full CSF panel (cell count with differential, glucose with paired serum, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, multiplex PCR panel, CSF lactate).

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone, or benzylpenicillin for this penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L, CLSI meningitis breakpoint); stop vancomycin if it was added.

ENT assessment of the left middle ear and mastoid as the probable source (recent otitis media, residual amber middle-ear effusion); temporal bone imaging and drainage only if ENT finds active otomastoiditis or he fails to improve.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis; sinus tachycardia expected in the context of fever and infection requires no separate ECG evaluation.
No clinical features suggestive of endocarditis as a primary source; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or management.
PET imaging has no diagnostic role in acute bacterial meningitis.
No seizure activity or persistent altered mental status to justify EEG in this alert, intact patient.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

differential.diagnosis: Acute otitis media with local complication (mastoiditis without meningitis)
differential.key_features: Recent left otitis media is the portal; excluded as the whole explanation: no mastoid tenderness or otorrhoea, and the meningeal syndrome with turbid neutrophilic CSF and pneumococcal bacteraemia establishes meningitis
Sudden headache with meningism; excluded: headache building over hours with fever 39.2 C, turbid CSF without xanthochromia, RBC 4 cells/microL
Subacute onset over days to weeks, lymphocytic CSF, basal enhancement; excluded: onset over hours, neutrophilic CSF, S. pneumoniae identified, no TB risk factors

key_clinical_evidence: Classic acute bacterial meningitis syndrome (fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia) with Gram-positive diplococci on CSF Gram stain and turbid neutrophilic CSF yields a high-confidence diagnosis; the critical diagnostic step is performing LP without delay.

Recent left otitis media is the likely portal of entry for S. pneumoniae, and the residual amber middle-ear effusion supports it. The portal is a source of the meningitis, not an alternative diagnosis; attributing the syndrome to an otitis relapse would defer the lumbar puncture and treatment.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Blood cultures must be obtained BEFORE the first antibiotic dose to preserve yield; empiric antibiotics must then follow immediately; every hour of delay increases mortality.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.18 is abnormally low (0.4 or less, WHO 2025 A.2.2); with a neutrophilic pleocytosis of 2840 cells/microL and protein of 289 mg/dL, the pattern is that of bacterial meningitis before Gram stain or culture results are available.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior otitis media is the likely pneumococcal portal of entry (parameningeal focus), not an alternative diagnosis. Completed antibiotic treatment does not exclude CNS seeding, which can occur during or after the otic infection. The full meningeal syndrome with turbid neutrophilic CSF, Gram-positive diplococci and S. pneumoniae on PCR defines the diagnosis as bacterial meningitis, and the ear history is epidemiologically explanatory rather than diagnostically reassuring.
red_herrings.data_point: Left acute otitis media treated with a 10-day amoxicillin course about 3 weeks ago, with reported resolution of ear pain
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the clinician toward a diagnosis of recurrent or incompletely treated otitis media or sinusitis, deferring or deprioritizing the meningitis evaluation on the assumption the current symptoms represent an otitic relapse.

labs.interpretation: Leukocytosis (WBC 22.1 x10^9/L) with marked neutrophilia (88%) and bandemia (9%). Mild hyponatremia (Sodium 132 mEq/L). Mild metabolic acidosis (Bicarbonate 21 mEq/L). CRP markedly elevated at 241 mg/L. Procalcitonin markedly elevated at 7.4 ng/mL. ESR elevated at 78 mm/hr. Lactate elevated at 2.8 mmol/L. Fibrinogen elevated at 418 mg/dL. D-dimer elevated at 1.2 mg/L FEU. Hemoglobin, renal function, liver function and coagulation indices otherwise within normal limits. HIV 1/2 Ag/Ab non-reactive.

clinical_pearls: Otitis media and mastoiditis are well-established parameningeal portals of entry for S. pneumoniae; apparent clinical resolution of the ear infection does not exclude intracranial seeding.

In an alert adult (GCS 15) without focal signs, cranial nerve deficit, papilledema, new seizure or severe immunocompromise, WHO 2025 section A.4 gives no indication for imaging before lumbar puncture; LP can and should proceed promptly.
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci on CSF Gram stain in the context of neutrophilic pleocytosis and critically low CSF glucose is effectively diagnostic of pneumococcal meningitis.
Dexamethasone reduces 8-week mortality in pneumococcal meningitis from approximately 34% to 14% when given before or with the first antibiotic dose (De Gans et al., NEJM 2002).
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: classic full meningeal syndrome with turbid neutrophilic CSF, Gram-positive diplococci on Gram stain and Streptococcus pneumoniae on PCR panel. Single clear diagnostic chain. GCS 15 with no WHO 2025 imaging-first criterion, so lumbar puncture proceeds without CT. One red herring (prior otitis media as anchor toward otitic relapse).
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required tools; 1 red herring; classic Gram-stain-positive presentation; no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion, so no CT before LP; single diagnostic chain to confident pneumococcal diagnosis

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Johnson is a 50-year-old right-handed man and warehouse forklift operator who presents to the emergency department at approximately 10:30 AM, brought by his wife after approximately 8 hours of worsening severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness. He reports waking at 2 AM with a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache, described as a constant, pounding pain rated 10 out of 10. He also noticed that turning on the bedroom lamp was unbearable and he pulled the sheets over his face. His wife measured a temperature of 38.8 degrees Celsius at home and gave him two tablets of acetaminophen, which did not relieve the headache. He is nauseated and vomited once before arrival. He has been unable to get comfortable and describes the back of his neck as feeling stiff and painful with any movement. He denies any recent head trauma, seizure activity, rash, or loss of consciousness. Importantly, he had a left-sided ear infection approximately three weeks ago, diagnosed by his primary care physician as acute otitis media, and was treated with a 10-day course of oral amoxicillin that he reports completing. He thought the ear infection had resolved, noting the ear pain improved, but he did not attend a follow-up appointment. He has not taken any antibiotics since completing that course. He denies any new ear pain or discharge today. On examination he is alert and oriented but clearly in significant distress, wincing with any light and holding his head still. Neck rigidity is marked. There are no focal motor or sensory deficits and no papilledema on fundoscopic examination.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity with pain and resistance on passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally: passive knee extension from 90-degree hip flexion elicits pain and resistance at approximately 120 degrees. Brudzinski sign positive: passive neck flexion produces bilateral involuntary hip flexion. No petechiae or purpura on full skin examination. No lymphadenopathy. No mastoid tenderness. Left tympanic membrane with mild amber discoloration without active bulging or purulent discharge.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and briskly reactive. Fundoscopic exam performed: optic discs sharp, no papilledema. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. Photophobia elicited with penlight; patient turns head away. Left ear canal clear on brief inspection; tympanic membrane with residual amber discoloration. Facial sensation grossly intact bilaterally. No facial asymmetry. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally by finger rub at bedside. Gag reflex intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient declines to ambulate due to headache and dizziness; brief assessment shows a narrow, steady stance.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time, though slow to respond and clearly in distress. GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). No focal cognitive deficits elicited on brief testing; however, concentration impaired due to severe pain. Speech fluent and appropriate.
